options: Casts the input to float32 on the GPU
Runs that op on the CPU
quiz.explain: Soft device placement (the default) falls back to a device that has a kernel for the op, usually the CPU.

glossary.def: One of the adjustable numbers inside a model. Training changes the weights; everything the model has learned is stored in them.
Short for loss function: the single number that says how wrong a model's guesses are on some examples. Training tries to push it down.
One building block of a neural network: it takes numbers in, does one kind of arithmetic with its own weights, and passes numbers on to the next layer.
The most common layer: every output is a weighted sum of every input plus a bias, followed by an activation function.
A simple non-linear function applied to each number a layer produces, such as ReLU (replace negatives with 0). Without it, stacked layers would collapse into one straight-line formula.
A function that turns a list of raw scores into probabilities: all positive and adding up to 1, with the biggest score getting the biggest share.
The raw scores a model outputs before softmax turns them into probabilities. Positive means 'more likely', but they are not yet between 0 and 1.
The recipe that uses gradients to update weights: plain gradient descent, or smarter variants such as Adam that adapt the step size per weight.
Running input through the model to get its output. The gradient is then worked out in a backward pass over the same steps.
A number that scores how well a model is doing, such as accuracy, tracked during training and evaluation. (Elsewhere, a metric is any number measured about a system over time.)
The share of predictions that were right, e.g. 0.95 means 95 out of 100 correct. The most common metric for classification.
A layer that, during training only, randomly switches off a fraction of its inputs, which makes the model rely less on any single number and overfit less.
A layer that rescales the numbers flowing through it to a steady average and spread, which makes training faster and more stable; it keeps running averages for use after training.
Making extra training examples by randomly altering real ones, e.g. flipping or cropping images, so the model sees more variety.
Turning raw data into the form a model wants: resizing images, scaling numbers to a small range, splitting text into words.
Filling shorter rows with a dummy value (often 0) so every row has the same length and fits in one rectangular tensor.
Representing a category as a list of zeros with a single 1 at that category's position, e.g. 'cat' among (dog, cat, bird) becomes [0, 1, 0].
TensorFlow's default way of running: each operation does its work the moment the Python line runs and returns a real value you can print.
A recorded description of a calculation: the operations and how their inputs and outputs connect, built once and then run many times, often faster than step-by-step Python.
Running a Python function once with stand-in tensors so TensorFlow can record every operation into a graph. Retracing is doing it again because the inputs' shapes or types changed.
A wrapper (used as @tf.function) that turns a Python function into a graph the first time it runs and reuses that graph afterwards.
TensorFlow's recorder: inside a `with tf.GradientTape()` block it notes every operation, so afterwards it can work out gradients by replaying them backwards.
Computing gradients automatically from the operations a program ran, instead of someone deriving the formula by hand.
How fast one quantity changes when another changes a tiny bit, e.g. the derivative of x squared is 2x. A gradient is a set of derivatives, one per input.
The full table of derivatives of every output with respect to every input (a Hessian is the same table for second derivatives).
Marked as something training may change. Non-trainable state, such as a step counter, is kept but never updated by gradients.
The high-level part of TensorFlow for building and training neural networks from ready-made layers, with model.fit() doing the training loop for you.
A plain container class for variables and tf.functions; Keras layers and models are special kinds of it, and saving tools know how to walk it.
The chain of steps that reads examples from memory or files, prepares them and hands them to the model in batches; in TensorFlow built with tf.data.
A holding area of N examples from which .shuffle() picks each next example at random, so the dataset need not fit in memory to be shuffled; bigger N means a more thorough mix.
Preparing the next batches in the background while the model is still busy with the current one, so the model never waits for data.
TensorFlow's own file format for storing many examples one after another in binary, which reads quickly from disk or network storage.
A tensor whose rows have different lengths, such as sentences with different word counts, stored as one flat list of values plus the row boundaries.
A tensor that is mostly zeros, stored as just the positions and values of the non-zero entries to save memory.
The chip a calculation runs on: a CPU, a GPU or a TPU. TensorFlow names them like /CPU:0 and /GPU:1.
Deciding which device each operation runs on. TensorFlow picks automatically (GPU if possible); soft placement falls back to the CPU when the GPU can't do an operation.
Google's custom chip built only for the matrix arithmetic of neural networks, available in Google Cloud; faster than GPUs for many models.
NVIDIA's software for running calculations on its GPUs; cuDNN is the companion library of fast neural-network routines. TensorFlow needs matching versions of both to use an NVIDIA GPU.
A setting that makes TensorFlow claim GPU memory bit by bit as needed, instead of reserving nearly all of it at start-up.
A saved copy of a model's variables (and other training state) at one moment, so training can be resumed from there instead of restarting.
TensorFlow's folder format for a finished model: the graphs, the variable values and named entry points, loadable without the Python code that built it.
A fixed description of what a function takes and returns: input names, shapes and dtypes. A SavedModel's named signatures are the entry points callers use.
TensorFlow's visual dashboard: a web page that plots the numbers training code logs, such as the loss over time, and compares runs.
The file TensorBoard reads: training code appends logged values (summaries) to it, each tagged with a name and a step number.
A TensorFlow object that decides how a model's variables and work are spread over several GPUs, TPUs or machines, so the rest of the training code stays the same.
One copy of the model running on one device during distributed training; each replica handles a slice of every batch.
Speeding up training by giving every device the full model and a different slice of each batch, then combining their gradients.
A step where every device shares its gradients with the others and each ends up with the combined (summed or averaged) result.
A machine whose job is to hold the model's variables; worker machines fetch them, compute gradients and send updates back, without waiting for each other.
The number of examples one training step sees across all devices together; each replica gets global batch divided by the number of replicas.
Doing most arithmetic with 16-bit floats (half the usual size, much faster on modern GPUs) while keeping the weights themselves in 32-bit so small updates aren't lost.
A 16-bit floating-point number: about 3 decimal digits of precision and a small range (largest value 65504). Fast on GPUs but easy to overflow or underflow.
A 16-bit float with the same range as float32 but fewer digits of precision; used on TPUs and newer GPUs because it rarely overflows.
When a number is too small for its type to represent and becomes 0 (the opposite of overflow); with float16, anything below about 0.00000006 vanishes.
Multiplying the loss by a large number before computing gradients so tiny gradients don't underflow in float16, then dividing them back before the update.
Special units in newer NVIDIA GPUs that multiply small 16-bit matrices extremely fast; the reason mixed precision gives big speedups.
TensorFlow's optimising compiler: it takes a whole graph and generates fast machine code for the CPU, GPU or TPU, merging many small operations into fewer big ones.
Merging several operations into one, so intermediate results stay in fast registers instead of being written to memory and read back between steps.
A tensor shape that is fully known when the code is compiled, as opposed to a dynamic shape that depends on the data (e.g. how many unique values an input has).
The slimmed-down version of TensorFlow for running trained models on phones, small devices and microcontrollers; models are converted to the compact .tflite file format.
Storing a model's numbers with fewer bits, e.g. 8-bit integers instead of 32-bit floats, so it is about 4 times smaller and faster, at a small cost in accuracy.
A few hundred typical inputs handed to the converter so it can measure the range of values flowing through the model and map them onto integers.
A LiteRT plug-in that hands supported operations to a faster chip on the device, such as the phone's GPU or neural accelerator.
In LiteRT, the small engine that loads a .tflite model and runs it. (In Python, the interpreter is the program that runs your source code line by line.)
A neural processing unit: a chip in many phones and small devices built only to run neural networks, usually needing integer (quantized) models.
A tiny, cheap computer-on-a-chip inside appliances and gadgets, with kilobytes rather than gigabytes of memory.
A ready-made server program that loads SavedModels and answers prediction requests over the network, with no Python needed in production.
A fast way for programs to call each other over the network using compact binary messages instead of JSON text; TF Serving offers it next to its REST API.
Letting the server collect requests that arrive at about the same time and run them through the model as one batch, which uses a GPU far better than one request at a time.
The part of tf.function that rewrites Python if/while/for statements into graph operations when their conditions depend on tensors.
Copying a loop body once per iteration instead of keeping a loop, e.g. a 3-step loop becomes three copies of its body in the graph.
A list-like container for tensors that works inside graph loops; you write to it by index and call stack() at the end to get one tensor.
One traced graph of a tf.function with fixed input shapes and dtypes. It never retraces; the polymorphic tf.function keeps one per signature it has seen.
TensorFlow's graph optimiser: before a graph runs, it folds constants, removes unused operations, merges patterns into fused kernels and so on.
Google's compact binary file format for structured data, with a schema; TensorFlow stores graphs (GraphDef) and SavedModels in it.
A hand-written formula for a function's gradient that TensorFlow uses instead of the one it would derive automatically, e.g. for numerical stability.
A trick for steps that have no useful gradient (like rounding): pretend the gradient is 1 so training can still flow through them.
One built-in TensorFlow operation, such as add, matmul or conv2d, with a registered name and typed inputs. Every tensor calculation is made of ops.
In TensorFlow, the actual code that carries out one op on one kind of device (CPU or GPU) for one dtype. (In an operating system, the kernel is instead its core program.)
Intra-op: how many threads one big op (like a matrix multiply) may use. Inter-op: how many independent ops may run at the same time.
An op you write yourself in C++ and load into TensorFlow when no built-in op does what you need.
